explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. "When the wine ran out…" is how the writer puts it. I think a wedding running out of wine is a rough spot, and I've had a cookie jar echo at me before. Sad sound.

Bread is a good guess, since a feast needs plenty. But this story never mentions bread. The text says the wine ran out, and that's what everything turns on. I'd have been nervous about my own cookie supply, honestly.
Oil never shows up in this scene, baker. The text says the wine ran out. Everything after that starts from one empty supply, and it isn't oil. Keep your eyes on the cups.
Yes, baker. Jesus' mother says to Him, "They have no more wine." She brings it straight to Him. Short and simple, no speech needed.
Simon Peter was one of the men Jesus called as disciples (John 1:40-42), so it's a fair guess. But the one who says it is Jesus' mother: "They have no more wine." She's the one who brings it to Him.

Nathanael is another man who came to Jesus earlier in John (John 1:45-49), so I see why he came to mind. This passage doesn't record him saying anything. Jesus' mother is the one who tells Him, "They have no more wine."

explanations.answer: She tells the servants to do whatever He says
explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. She turns to the servants and says, "Do whatever He tells you." Jesus has just said His hour hasn't come yet, and she still points the servants to Him. I think that's some serious trust.

explanations.answer: She asks the bridegroom to send for more
explanations.explanation: That sounds like a plan, but the text never has her go to the bridegroom. She speaks to the servants instead. Her words are "Do whatever He tells you." I'd have started counting my own cookies in a panic, so she's already ahead of me.

explanations.answer: She sits back down and lets it go
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't show her sitting back down. She turns to the servants and says, "Do whatever He tells you." She keeps moving after Jesus' answer.

Right, baker. Jesus tells the servants, "Fill the jars with water." Those six stone jars had been set there for the Jewish rites of purification. Each could hold from twenty to thirty gallons (John 2:6). So the servants had a lot of filling to do, and they filled them to the brim.
The text goes the other direction. Jesus doesn't tell them to empty anything. He says, "Fill the jars with water." Filling is the job here, not pouring out.

No carrying of jars in this story, baker. Jesus tells the servants, "Fill the jars with water." The bridegroom only comes up later, when the master of the banquet calls him aside. Those jars were big enough that I'd need a forklift anyway.
Not quite, baker. The text says "So they filled them to the brim." That means all the way to the top, not halfway. These servants don't cut corners.
Yes, it's false. The text says, "So they filled them to the brim." Six jars, each able to hold from twenty to thirty gallons, all filled to the top.
Not this time, baker. The text says the master of the banquet "…did not know where it was from…" He tastes it and has no idea how it got there. It's the people who carried the water who know.
That's right. The master of the banquet "…did not know where it was from…" He just tastes it and gets to be impressed. The text says the servants who had drawn the water knew.
Yes, baker. The text says "…the servants who had drawn the water knew." They drew the water, and they knew where it was from. I'd love to have seen their faces.
The disciples are at the wedding, but the text doesn't say they drew the water. It says "…the servants who had drawn the water knew." The ones who drew the water are the ones who knew.

Guests are a fair guess, baker. The text says the servants who had drawn the water knew where the wine came from. The master of the banquet didn't know, and the text doesn't say the guests did either.

explanations.answer: Saved the fine wine until now
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The master of the banquet says, "But you have saved the fine wine until now!" Everyone else brings out the good stuff first. He sounds shocked, and I would be too if my last cookie tasted better than my first.

explanations.answer: Gave every guest a second cup
explanations.explanation: Second cups never come up in this story. The master of the banquet says to the bridegroom, "But you have saved the fine wine until now!" His surprise is about when the fine wine shows up, which is late.

The text never says the bridegroom pours anything. What the master of the banquet says is, "But you have saved the fine wine until now!" His surprise is about the order of the wine, not who held the pitcher.
True, baker. The text says Jesus revealed His glory, "…and His disciples believed in Him." This is called the first of His signs. Their belief is right there in the verse.
Not false, baker. The text says Jesus "…revealed His glory, and His disciples believed in Him." That's said about the first of His signs at Cana. So the answer is True.
Right, baker. After this, Jesus went down to Capernaum with His mother and brothers and His disciples. They stayed a few days. Quite a crowd for a short visit.
Bethsaida is a real town in this Gospel, the hometown of Philip (John 1:44). But this passage doesn't send Jesus there. He goes down to Capernaum after the wedding.
Nazareth does come up in John, where Philip calls Him "Jesus of Nazareth" (John 1:45). But after the wedding, the text says Jesus went down to Capernaum. That's where the group stays a few days.
